Read each architecture/dataset group against its own ordinary baseline. The first two groups use clean MNIST; the last retrains LeNet on the ambiguous Dirty-MNIST distribution introduced below. Arrows identify the preferred direction. The uncertainty entries and ROC plots use the same saved probabilities and score definitions. Every entry is a mean ± standard deviation across three training seeds, not a confidence interval.

The four panels in the PDF are column groups of this single comparison table; they repeat the model, dataset and method so quality can be read alongside cost without shrinking the type. The following figures show the predeclared seed 41 diagnostics and all three seeds’ learning curves.

if (exists("mnist_runs")) {
mnist_diagnostic(mnist_runs,"mlp")
mnist_learning(mnist_runs,"mlp")

} else recorded_cell(76)

Recorded benchmark output; no new training in this reading-mode execution.

The MLP makes the distinction between classification accuracy and probability quality visible. Over three paired seeds, ordinary Adam gives 97.89% / 0.07150 NLL, moment MFVI 98.37% / 0.05238, and moment power-EP 98.45% / 0.05067. Their ECE values are 0.56%, 0.33%, and 0.26%, respectively. The ordinary model’s validation NLL turns upward while accuracy changes little. Its reported test result nevertheless uses the earlier validation-selected checkpoint, not the overfit endpoint.

The ROC curves answer two separate questions: whether low confidence finds classification mistakes, and whether it distinguishes Fashion-MNIST from MNIST. The common score is one minus maximum class probability. Moment MFVI and EP improve Fashion AUROC from 0.744 to 0.923 and 0.920. The plotted seed is fixed at 41; the table includes all three seeds. Calibration bins with fewer than 20 examples are omitted from the curve, but every example contributes to the table’s ECE. Larger markers indicate more examples in a bin. The ordinary MLP’s very confident Fashion predictions explain why its good clean-image accuracy coexists with much weaker OOD detection.

Sampled MFVI has the lowest NLL here (0.04623). Thus the useful moment predictor is still an approximation, not numerically identical Bayesian averaging. In this R implementation, moment MFVI/EP require 4.61×/6.20× the ordinary training time and 3.43×/3.73× its prediction time. The clocks include the declared covariance and optimizer calculations; earlier optimized PyTorch timings are not substituted. These results demonstrate improved prediction and uncertainty under the stated protocol, while keeping the approximation and its computational price visible.

if (exists("mnist_runs")) {
mnist_diagnostic(mnist_runs,"lenet")
mnist_learning(mnist_runs,"lenet")

} else recorded_cell(78)

Recorded benchmark output; no new training in this reading-mode execution.

LeNet carries the same comparison through convolution and max-pooling. Ordinary Adam gives 98.86% accuracy / 0.03892 NLL; moment MFVI gives 99.15% / 0.02506, and moment power-EP 99.12% / 0.02849. ECE decreases from 0.52% to 0.22% and 0.33%, respectively. Both moment models also improve Brier score and selective risk. Their Fashion-MNIST AUROCs are 0.982 and 0.980, compared with 0.970 for ordinary LeNet. The convolutional baseline already distinguishes these datasets much better than the plain MLP; Bayesian gains need not have the same size across architectures or metrics.

The sampled controls help interpret the approximation. Sampled MFVI reaches 99.25% / 0.02297, while sampled EP reaches 99.09% / 0.02702. Thus moment prediction retains a useful Bayesian improvement without matching every sampled score. These are separately learned beliefs; the table is a performance comparison, not a same-belief moment-error measurement.

Native moment prediction takes 0.221 s (MFVI) or 0.227 s (EP) for 10,000 images, versus 0.347 s / 0.351 s for the sampled controls and 0.053 s for the ordinary model. The complete R training runs take about 331 s / 328 s, compared with 43 s for ordinary LeNet: approximately 7.6×. These TensorFlow timings are reported directly; the faster historical PyTorch implementation is a different measurement.

Dirty-MNIST asks a different question

Clean MNIST is joined with the released Ambiguous-MNIST images and their multiple labels. This extension trains LeNet on 55,000 clean and 55,000 ambiguous label pairs, reserving 5,000 of each for validation. All ten labels of an ambiguous image remain in the same split. Fashion-MNIST is still OOD; ambiguous digits are in distribution. We preserve the clean experiment’s [0,1] pixels and do not add input noise, explicitly differing from the DDU loader’s normalized/noisy default. See the authors’ loader. Classification metrics count 10,000 clean examples and 60,000 ambiguous label pairs. OOD metrics instead count 16,000 unique ID images against 10,000 Fashion-MNIST images; ten labels do not create ten distinct OOD observations. Ambiguous label pairs make up one half of validation but six sevenths of the test mixture, so validation and test accuracy/NLL have different difficulty.

Accuracy has a different scale here. If an image’s ten labels have empirical frequencies rcr_c, any fixed prediction gets at most max⁡crc\max_c r_c of those labels right. Its average log loss is −∑crclog⁡pc=H(r)+KL⁡(r‖p)≥H(r)-\sum_c r_c\log p_c=H(r)+\operatorname{KL}(r\Vert p)\ge H(r). The released test labels therefore give an accuracy upper bound of 86.03% and an NLL lower bound of 0.32993 for the combined 70,000 label pairs. These are finite-label diagnostics, not population Bayes limits or quantities used for fitting or selecting any model. They explain why Dirty-MNIST scores should not be compared directly with clean MNIST’s 99% accuracy.

Total predictive entropy is H(p‾)H(\bar p). For a Bayesian belief, the additional decomposition I[y,W∣x,D]=H(p‾)−Eq[H(pW)]I[y,W\mid x,D]=H(\bar p)-E_q[H(p_W)] measures model disagreement. For moment prediction this uses the same Gaussian-head nodes and is a closure-based approximation. A single point network has zero such disagreement by construction, so the common OOD comparison uses predictive entropy or maximum probability, because MI is zero for a point weight distribution. The distinction is to separate ambiguity from unfamiliar inputs, rather than expect every uncertainty measure to increase on the same images. The two-panel illustration uses moment MFVI and the predeclared seed 41. A curve farther to the right means larger uncertainty. The combined table and ROC plots retain all five methods.

if (exists("mnist_runs")) {
labels <- mnist_runs[[1]]$ambiguous_labels
frequency <- t(apply(labels,1,function(y)tabulate(y+1L,nbins=10L)/length(y)))
label_limits <- c(accuracy_upper=(10000+60000*mean(apply(frequency,1,max)))/70000,
  nll_lower=60000*mean(-rowSums(frequency*log(pmax(frequency,1e-30))))/70000)
print(round(label_limits,5))
mnist_diagnostic(mnist_runs,"lenet","dirty")
mnist_ambiguity(mnist_runs)

} else recorded_cell(81)

Recorded benchmark output; no new training in this reading-mode execution.
accuracy_upper      nll_lower
       0.86029        0.32993

Across three seeds, ordinary LeNet obtains 82.73% accuracy / 0.50539 NLL on the combined clean/ambiguous test labels. Moment MFVI gives 83.40% / 0.48536, and moment power-EP 83.21% / 0.49049. Their ECE values are 1.53%, 1.25%, and 1.31%, respectively. These scores are on the ambiguity-aware scale derived above, not clean MNIST’s 99% scale. Sampled MFVI gives 83.55% / 0.48290; sampled EP gives 83.14% / 0.49209. The moment approximations therefore retain the main predictive improvement without matching every sampled result.

With unfamiliar Fashion images as the positive class, AUROC increases from 0.860 for ordinary LeNet to 0.902 for moment MFVI and 0.897 for moment EP. This test now includes ambiguous digits among the ID images; its difficulty differs from the clean-only OOD test. The seed variation is shown in the combined table, including MFVI’s 0.027 AUROC standard deviation. Three seeds support this measured example, not a claim that Bayesian uncertainty always dominates on every dataset.

The two-panel illustration asks what uncertainty means for the same learned moment-MFVI belief. Ambiguous digits have greater predictive entropy than clean digits. Fashion images shift farther toward both high total uncertainty and high model disagreement. The quantities answer different questions: entropy includes ambiguity, while disagreement measures variation across the approximate Bayesian predictions. Neither is an exact oracle for the source of an individual image’s uncertainty.

Training the moment MFVI/EP models takes 652 s / 643 s, versus 86 s for ordinary LeNet. Their measured prediction times remain 0.220 s / 0.245 s per 10,000 clean images, versus 0.052 s for the ordinary model and 0.328 s / 0.333 s for the sampled controls. These throughput measurements use the same clean-image workload for all three experiment groups; the Dirty-MNIST quality metrics use the full combined test set.

5. CIFAR-10: ResNet and DenseNet

The CIFAR experiments reuse the layer operations, shared graph traversal, objectives and metric functions already introduced. Residual addition and dense concatenation reuse the same uncertain ancestors. Covariance directions retain that dependence; diagonal projection deliberately discards some of it. Architectures are CIFAR ResNet-20 and DenseNet-40, growth 12.

The full schedule is 100 epochs, with a fixed stratified 45,000/5,000 fit/stopping split, batch 125, train-only crop/flip augmentation and the official test set for reporting. Recorded settings are printed with each table. BatchNorm buffers are committed once per minibatch. Paired initial means, preprocessing and data order support the within-protocol comparison; optimizers and numerical moment approximations remain explicitly labelled.

The exact finite EP and canonical MFVI updates in Section 2 establish their Gaussian inference meanings. The larger benchmarks use the recorded Vadam or Adam variants below; the coordinate theorem does not assert these optimizers are the same finite update.

EP: explicit sites and the scalable tied energy

Ordinary EP keeps q∝p0∏nf̃nq\propto p_0\prod_n\widetilde f_n. Remove site nn in information coordinates, form the tilted distribution q\nfn/Znq^{\setminus n}f_n/Z_n, project its moments, and replace the removed site by qproj/q\nq_{\mathrm{proj}}/q^{\setminus n}. Repeatedly multiplying by fnf_n without removal is not EP. The implementation’s Gaussian checks implement this literal procedure separately from the large-network approximation.

Storing NN dense parameter sites is not a sensible transformer implementation. Our large-network tied power-EP energy uses k=α/Nk=\alpha/N, qc=q1−kp0k/Aαq_c=q^{1-k}p_0^k/A_\alpha, Aα=∫q1−kp0kA_\alpha=\int q^{1-k}p_0^k, and minimizes Fα(q)=−τα{1N∑nlogEqcp(yn∣xn,w)α/τ+logAα}. F_\alpha(q)=-\frac{\tau}{\alpha}\left\{ \frac1N\sum_n\log E_{q_c}p(y_n\mid x_n,w)^{\alpha/\tau} +\log A_\alpha\right\}. It is not claimed identical to sequential untied EP. Its minibatch estimator averages the first term over the batch and includes the external field once; its strength does not decrease when the number of minibatches changes.

For one coordinate let d=1+k(v/v0−1)d=1+k(v/v_0-1). Completing the Gaussian square gives vc=v/dv_c=v/d, mc=m0+(1−k)(m−m0)/dm_c=m_0+(1-k)(m-m_0)/d, and −log⁡Aα=12∑i[logdi−klog(vi/v0i)+k(1−k)(mi−m0i)2v0idi]. -\log A_\alpha=\tfrac12\sum_i\left[ \log d_i-k\log(v_i/v_{0i})+ \frac{k(1-k)(m_i-m_{0i})^2}{v_{0i}d_i}\right]. Derivation. The product precision is (1−k)/v+k/v0=d/v(1-k)/v+k/v_0=d/v. Its information parameter is (1−k)m/v+km0/v0(1-k)m/v+km_0/v_0. The Gaussian integral supplies the determinant factor d−1/2(v/v0)k/2d^{-1/2}(v/v_0)^{k/2}; subtracting the completed-square constant gives the stated distance term. Products across coordinates turn the logarithm into the displayed sum. ∎

As α↓0\alpha\downarrow0, differentiating log⁡Eqexp⁡{α(log⁡p0−log⁡q)/N}\log E_q\exp\{\alpha(\log p_0-\log q)/N\} at zero gives −KL(q‖p0)/N-\mathrm{KL}(q\Vert p_0)/N. The likelihood log-normalizer derivative is Eqlog⁡p(yn∣xn,w)/τE_q\log p(y_n\mid x_n,w)/\tau; the cavity-density derivative cancels its normalizer derivative. Therefore Fα→−N−1∑nEqlog⁡p(yn∣xn,w)+τKL/NF_\alpha\to-N^{-1}\sum_nE_q\log p(y_n\mid x_n,w)+\tau\mathrm{KL}/N. This limit checks prior accounting, not global convergence.

Match the notation to the executable controls. The code calls the likelihood power α/τ\alpha/\tau power, and calls τ\tau tau; it passes alpha = tau * power into power_cavity. The reproduced EP configurations use power = 1, so their head averages ordinary class probabilities while the cavity removal fraction is τ/N\tau/N. Varying tau with power fixed is therefore not the α↓0\alpha\downarrow0 limit at fixed τ\tau just proved. This distinction prevents a regularization sweep from being mislabelled an EP-to-VI limit.

The CIFAR configurations use ordinary AdamW, Vadam for MFVI, and Adam on Gaussian means/log variances for tied power-EP. These optimizers act after the shared moment calculation; Vadam is not required by the Gaussian identities.

For the reference Vadam recurrence write $N_{\rm eff}=N/\tau$, prior precision pi=1/v0ip_i=1/v_{0i} and $\lambda_i=p_i/N_{\rm eff}$. With likelihood-gradient moments ai=E[gi]a_i=E[g_i] and bi=E[gi2]b_i=E[g_i^2], its temporal state updates are ri+=β1ri+(1−β1)[ai+λi(mi−m0i)],si+=β2si+(1−β2)bi. r_i^+=\beta_1r_i+(1-\beta_1)[a_i+\lambda_i(m_i-m_{0i})],\qquad s_i^+=\beta_2s_i+(1-\beta_2)b_i. Then mi+=mi−ηr̂i/(ŝi+λi)m_i^+=m_i-\eta\widehat r_i/(\sqrt{\widehat s_i}+\lambda_i) and $v_i^+=1/(N_{\rm eff}s_i^++p_i)$, where hats denote the reference’s bias correction. Its initial $s_i=(v_i^{-1}-p_i)/N_{\rm eff}$ preserves the declared initial belief variance. This initialization is part of the reproduced algorithm, not a zero-state Adam replacement.

For sampled MFVI, average gig_i and gi2g_i^2 separately across complete network draws. For moment MFVI, the reference uses bi≈ai2+(HDiag⁡ve)i2b_i\approx a_i^2+(H\sqrt{\operatorname{Diag}v}\,e)_i^2 with one fixed Rademacher direction and the point-loss Hessian HH. To derive the contraction, linearize g(w)≈g(m)+H(w−m)g(w)\approx g(m)+H(w-m); independence and E[ee⊤]=IE[ee^\top]=I give Ee[(HDiag⁡ve)i2]=(HDiag⁡(v)H⊤)iiE_e[(H\sqrt{\operatorname{Diag}v}\,e)_i^2]=(H\operatorname{Diag}(v)H^\top)_{ii}. A single fixed direction is an approximation to that expectation, not an exact second moment. This statistic differs from the VI variance derivative and needs its own validation. The EP optimizer instead consumes the differentiated cavity likelihood and external field in (m,log⁡v)(m,\log v); it does not replace posterior variance by Adam’s squared-gradient accumulator.

The text reproductions also retain the reference’s separate, zero-initialized likelihood normalization state ui+=β2ui+(1−β2)biu_i^+=\beta_2u_i+(1-\beta_2)b_i. When that recorded option is active, the mean denominator uses ûi+λi\sqrt{\widehat u_i}+\lambda_i, while the posterior variance still uses $1/(N_{\rm eff}s_i+p_i)$. The initial prior-compatible sis_i and the temporal normalizer uiu_i have different roles. The code records this choice in configure_text_belief; silently identifying these two states changes the training trajectory even when the sampled gradients are identical.

Native Keras summaries and complete architecture downloads

These are framework-generated views of executable models. Keras draws the R/TensorFlow graphs and prints their native layer summaries. The four selected summaries throughout Sections 5–7 give output shapes and parameter counts by architectural block. Each downloadable fully expanded model PDF shows every registered layer, branch and tensor shape. These vector PDFs remain sharp when zoomed; the complete graph fits on its own page. A full text summary is also linked.

The benchmark implementation stores explicit TensorFlow operations rather than a Keras Model. The small inspection adapter exposes those same callbacks, parent edges and weight-mean variables as nested Keras models. It does not implement a second convolution, attention or residual network. Comparing all 674 operations and all five model outputs gives zero discrepancy on the recorded float32 execution checks. Transformer input length is dynamic; both five- and eight-token checks pass.

The diagrams inspect the mean forward graph. Gaussian log variances and the moment/pseudo-gradient calculation remain the separate belief state and algorithm described earlier. Native parameter counts include frozen storage and BatchNorm buffers; they do not include the separate log-variance arrays. GPT-2’s count also includes its cached two-row verbalizer tensor. These are architecture checks at seeded/public initialization, not new performance evaluations.

All five views use tf.keras.utils.plot_model and Model.summary. The short R invocation is:

view <- keras_inspection(g, example)
view$model$summary(expand_nested=FALSE)
tf$keras$utils$plot_model(view$model, "expanded.pdf",
                         show_shapes=TRUE, show_layer_names=TRUE,
                         expand_nested=TRUE)

Set REBUILD_MODEL_VIEWS=TRUE with public downloads enabled to regenerate the native summaries and PDFs using these same definitions. All downloads are included in the package and work offline after extraction. The export scales oversized pages as a whole; it does not crop the graph or turn it into a bitmap.

ResNet-20 / CIFAR-10

Three stages each contain three residual blocks. The stage-transition shortcut uses stride-two subsampling and channel padding (option A).

Download fully expanded model (PDF) · Full native layer summary.

# %% Residual and dense image networks: ordinary and moment paths share the graph
normal <- function(dims,scale,dtype=tf$float32) tf$random$normal(as.integer(dims),stddev=scale,dtype=dtype)
conv_node <- function(g,x,cin,cout,k=3L,stride=1L,name) {
  force(x) # Materialize a nested parent before registering this layer's weights.
  stride<-as.integer(stride)
  w<-weight(g,paste0(name,"_W"),normal(c(k,k,cin,cout),sqrt(2/(k*k*cin))))
  # PyTorch's k//2 padding is symmetric, including at stride two. TensorFlow
  # SAME would pad even-size inputs asymmetrically and shift the residual path.
  pad<-as.integer(k%/%2L)
  op<-function(xs,ws)tf$nn$conv2d(
    tf$pad(xs[[1]],list(c(0L,0L),c(pad,pad),c(pad,pad),c(0L,0L))),ws[[1]],
    strides=as.integer(c(1,stride,stride,1)),padding="VALID")
  node(g,name,x,op,w,kind="conv")
}
relu_node <- function(g,x,name) node(g,name,x,function(xs,ws)tf$nn$relu(xs[[1]]),kind="relu")
add_node <- function(g,a,b,name) node(g,name,c(a,b),function(xs,ws)xs[[1]]+xs[[2]])
concat_node <- function(g,a,b,name) node(g,name,c(a,b),function(xs,ws)tf$concat(xs,axis=-1L))
bn_node <- function(g,x,c,name) {
  force(x)
  gamma<-weight(g,paste0(name,"_gamma"),tf$ones(as.integer(c)),variance=1e-5)
  beta<-weight(g,paste0(name,"_beta"),tf$zeros(as.integer(c)),variance=1e-5)
  running<-new.env(parent=emptyenv())
  running$m<-tf$Variable(tf$zeros(as.integer(c)),trainable=FALSE)
  running$v<-tf$Variable(tf$ones(as.integer(c)),trainable=FALSE)
  i<-node(g,name,x,function(xs,ws) {
    a<-xs[[1]]
    if(isTRUE(g$training)) {
      m<-tf$reduce_mean(a,axis=as.integer(c(0,1,2)),keepdims=TRUE)
      v<-tf$reduce_mean(tf$square(a-m),axis=as.integer(c(0,1,2)),keepdims=TRUE)
    } else {m<-running$m;v<-running$v}
    (a-m)*tf$math$rsqrt(v+1e-5)*ws[[1]]+ws[[2]]
  },c(gamma,beta),kind="bn")
  g$nodes[[i-1L]]$normalization<-running
  i
}
norm_statistics <- function(g,states,moment=FALSE) {
  # Training normalizes with biased batch variance, but the stored running
  # variance uses the unbiased estimate, exactly as the reference BatchNorm.
  result<-list()
  for(op in g$nodes) if(!is.null(op$normalization)) {
    a<-states[[op$parents[[1]]]]
    if(moment)a<-a$m
    m<-tf$reduce_mean(a,axis=as.integer(c(0,1,2)))
    v<-tf$reduce_mean(tf$square(a-m),axis=as.integer(c(0,1,2)))
    n<-tf$cast(tf$size(a)/tf$gather(tf$shape(a),3L),a$dtype)
    result[[length(result)+1L]]<-list(m=m,v=v*n/(n-1))
  }
  result
}
commit_statistics <- function(g,statistics) {
  j<-0L
  for(op in g$nodes) if(!is.null(op$normalization)) {
    j<-j+1L
    op$normalization$m$assign(.9*op$normalization$m+.1*statistics[[j]]$m)
    op$normalization$v$assign(.9*op$normalization$v+.1*statistics[[j]]$v)
  }
}
commit_norm <- function(g,states,moment=FALSE) {
  commit_statistics(g,norm_statistics(g,states,moment))
}
dense_node <- function(g,x,cin,cout,name,readout=FALSE,initial_scale=sqrt(2/cin),
                       variance=1e-5,prior_variance=1e-3) {
  force(x)
  w<-weight(g,paste0(name,"_W"),normal(c(cin,cout),initial_scale),variance,prior_variance)
  b<-weight(g,paste0(name,"_b"),tf$zeros(as.integer(cout)),variance,prior_variance)
  node(g,name,x,function(xs,ws)tf$matmul(xs[[1]],ws[[1]])+ws[[2]],c(w,b),
       kind=if(readout)"gaussian_readout" else "delta")
}
build_cifar <- function(architecture="resnet20",rank=4L,seed=41L) {
  tf$random$set_seed(as.integer(seed));g<-new_graph(rank,seed);g$training<-FALSE
  # Recompute local derivatives for the dense graph; same moments and updates.
  g$recompute_moments<-architecture=="densenet40"
  g$prior_center<-"zero"
  if(architecture=="resnet20") {
    x<-relu_node(g,bn_node(g,conv_node(g,1L,3L,16L,name="stem"),16L,"stem_bn"),"stem_relu")
    cin<-16L
    for(stage in 1:3) for(block in 1:3) {
      cout<-c(16L,32L,64L)[[stage]];s<-if(stage>1 && block==1) 2L else 1L
      p<-paste0("stage",stage,"_block",block)
      skip<-x
      if(s==2L) {
        pad<-cin/2L
        skip<-node(g,paste0(p,"_shortcut"),x,local({pad<-pad;function(xs,ws) {
          a<-tf$strided_slice(xs[[1]],begin=c(0L,0L,0L,0L),end=tf$shape(xs[[1]]),
                             strides=c(1L,2L,2L,1L))
          tf$pad(a,list(c(0L,0L),c(0L,0L),c(0L,0L),as.integer(c(pad,pad))))
        }}))
      }
      h<-conv_node(g,x,cin,cout,stride=s,name=paste0(p,"_conv1"))
      h<-relu_node(g,bn_node(g,h,cout,paste0(p,"_bn1")),paste0(p,"_relu1"))
      h<-bn_node(g,conv_node(g,h,cout,cout,name=paste0(p,"_conv2")),cout,paste0(p,"_bn2"))
      x<-relu_node(g,add_node(g,skip,h,paste0(p,"_sum")),paste0(p,"_relu2"));cin<-cout
    }
  } else {
    stopifnot(architecture=="densenet40")
    cin<-16L;x<-conv_node(g,1L,3L,cin,name="stem")
    for(stage in 1:3) {
      for(block in 1:12) {
        p<-paste0("dense",stage,"_",block)
        h<-relu_node(g,bn_node(g,x,cin,paste0(p,"_bn")),paste0(p,"_relu"))
        h<-conv_node(g,h,cin,12L,name=paste0(p,"_conv"))
        x<-concat_node(g,x,h,paste0(p,"_concat"));cin<-cin+12L
      }
      if(stage<3) {
        p<-paste0("transition",stage)
        x<-relu_node(g,bn_node(g,x,cin,paste0(p,"_bn")),paste0(p,"_relu"))
        x<-conv_node(g,x,cin,cin,k=1L,name=paste0(p,"_conv"))
        x<-node(g,paste0(p,"_pool"),x,function(xs,ws)tf$nn$avg_pool2d(xs[[1]],2L,2L,"VALID"))
      }
    }
    x<-relu_node(g,bn_node(g,x,cin,"final_bn"),"final_relu")
  }
  x<-node(g,"global_pool",x,function(xs,ws)tf$reduce_mean(xs[[1]],axis=c(1L,2L)))
  dense_node(g,x,cin,10L,"classifier",readout=TRUE)
  g$architecture<-architecture;g
}

if(RUN_CIFAR_TRAINING) {
  recorded_out<-OUT;OUT<-file.path(OUT,"cifar_fresh")
  dir.create(OUT,recursive=TRUE,showWarnings=FALSE)
  for(task in c("resnet20_cifar10","densenet40_cifar10"))
    for(method in c("ordinary","sampled_mfvi","moment_mfvi","sampled_ep","moment_ep"))
      train_one(task,method,41L)
  files<-list.files(OUT,pattern="^evaluation[.]rds$",recursive=TRUE,full.names=TRUE)
  tutorial_records<-lapply(files,function(file) {
    a<-readRDS(file);o<-file.path(dirname(file),"ood_predictions.rds")
    list(p=a$probabilities,y=a$labels,label=a$method,family=a$benchmark,result=a,file=file,
         ood=if(file.exists(o))readRDS(o)$p else NULL)
  })
  curves<-do.call(rbind,lapply(tutorial_records,function(r) {
    h<-do.call(rbind,r$result$history)
    data.frame(family=r$family,label=r$label,seed=r$result$seed,epoch=h$epoch,
      training_seconds=h$training_seconds,validation_nll=h$stopping_nll,validation_accuracy=h$stopping_accuracy)
  }))
  write.csv(curves,file.path(OUT,"new_learning_curves.csv"),row.names=FALSE)
}

6. Transformers: GPT-2 and LoRA

Conditional Gaussian carriers and probability averaging

The BLoB-inspired construction learns one diagonal Gaussian adapter distribution, not a mixture or an ensemble: A=MA+ρ⊙2⊙ϵA=M_A+\rho^{\odot2}\odot\epsilon with ϵ∼N(0,I)\epsilon\sim N(0,I); BB is a point parameter and the pretrained backbone is frozen. Thus Var⁡(A)=ρ⊙4\operatorname{Var}(A)=\rho^{\odot4}. The objective is expected log likelihood plus the source Gaussian KL, with prior standard deviation 0.2 and the source cyclic KL schedule. Likelihood AdamW and the separate prior/variance SGD step follow that source update. This is mean-field VI with a conditional-moment approximation, not EP or a canonical unit MFVI step.

Why activation correlations survive diagonal weights. For one adapter, write z=(W+sBA)xz=(W+sBA)x and W¯=W+sBMA\overline W=W+sBM_A. With independent AA and xx, mean mxm_x and covariance CxC_x, conditional expectation gives E[z]=W¯mxE[z]=\overline Wm_x. The law of total covariance gives the exact affine identity Cov⁡(z)=W¯CxW¯⊤+s2BDiag⁡{VA(diag⁡Cx+mx⊙2)}B⊤\operatorname{Cov}(z)=\overline W C_x\overline W^\top +s^2B\operatorname{Diag}\{V_A(\operatorname{diag}C_x+m_x^{\odot2})\}B^\top, where VA=Var⁡(A)V_A=\operatorname{Var}(A). To derive the second term, condition on xx: independent rows of AA have conditional output variance ∑j(VA)ijxj2\sum_j(V_A)_{ij}x_j^2; then average xj2x_j^2. Multiplication by BB induces correlated outputs even though VAV_A is diagonal. For different inputs, the same random adapter is reused; their injected cross-covariance contains ∑j(VA)ijE[xjx′j]\sum_j(V_A)_{ij}E[x_jx'_j], not separate weight draws.

The training approximation retains these dependencies through shared local directions. For paired nonlinear block outputs Yk±Y_k^\pm, define their mean m=(2K)−1∑k(Yk++Yk−)m=(2K)^{-1}\sum_k(Y_k^++Y_k^-), odd deviations Ok=(Yk+−Yk−)/2O_k=(Y_k^+-Y_k^-)/2 and even deviations Ek=(Yk++Yk−)/2−mE_k=(Y_k^++Y_k^-)/2-m. A moment carrier Ỹ=m+K−1/2∑k(ϵkOk+ζkEk)\widetilde Y=m+K^{-1/2}\sum_k(\epsilon_kO_k+\zeta_kE_k), with independent coefficient vectors uniformly distributed on the sphere of radius K\sqrt K, has conditional mean mm and covariance K−1∑k(OkOk⊤+EkEk⊤)K^{-1}\sum_k(O_kO_k^\top+E_kE_k^\top). Indeed, ϵ=Kg/∥g∥\epsilon=\sqrt K g/\|g\| for g∼N(0,IK)g\sim N(0,I_K) satisfies Eϵ=0E\epsilon=0 and E[ϵϵ⊤]=IKE[\epsilon\epsilon^\top]=I_K by rotational symmetry and its fixed squared norm KK; the independently generated ζ\zeta does too. Expanding the paired centered outer products proves that this equals the paired empirical covariance. Two antithetic pairs per block were used in the training fit. This spherical carrier is stochastic and need not be Gaussian conditional on its integration nodes; the finite-node nonlinear calculation remains an approximation. The posterior weights are still a single Gaussian. The Gaussian coordinate bridge remains the same; this extension changes the moment closure and update.

At deployment, a compact fixed Gaussian state carries correlated directions through the network. SST-2 uses nonlinear rank 1; CLINC uses tangent rank 2. The output head averages probabilities: for SST-2 it integrates E[σ(D)]E[\sigma(D)] over the Gaussian logit contrast; for CLINC it averages softmax probabilities at symmetric output nodes. It does not take softmax of mean logits.

Implementation. The transformer fits in this comparison use the original Python/PyTorch sources included below and in python/blob_mirror/. Their derivations and numerical records are in advanced_results/compact_transformers/. The R reporting cells compute the common metrics and plots from those predictions. R model constructors are included separately for the layer and architecture calculations.

layer_norm <- function(x,gamma,beta,eps) {
  m<-tf$reduce_mean(x,axis=-1L,keepdims=TRUE)
  v<-tf$reduce_mean(tf$square(x-m),axis=-1L,keepdims=TRUE)
  (x-m)*tf$math$rsqrt(v+scalar(eps,x))*gamma+beta
}
split_heads <- function(x) {
  s<-tf$shape(x)
  tf$transpose(tf$reshape(x,tf$stack(list(tf$gather(s,0L),tf$gather(s,1L),12L,64L))),c(0L,2L,1L,3L))
}
merge_heads <- function(x) {
  s<-tf$shape(x)
  tf$reshape(tf$transpose(x,c(0L,2L,1L,3L)),tf$stack(list(tf$gather(s,0L),tf$gather(s,2L),768L)))
}
attention <- function(q,k,v,inputs,causal=FALSE) {
  q<-split_heads(q);k<-split_heads(k);v<-split_heads(v)
  a<-tf$matmul(q,k,transpose_b=TRUE)/8
  mask<-tf$gather(inputs,1L,axis=2L)
  a<-a+(1-tf$expand_dims(tf$expand_dims(mask,1L),1L))*(-1e4)
  if(causal) {
    T<-tf$gather(tf$shape(a),3L)
    lower<-tf$linalg$band_part(tf$ones(tf$stack(list(T,T)),dtype=a$dtype),-1L,0L)
    a<-a+(1-lower)*(-1e4)
  }
  merge_heads(tf$matmul(tf$nn$softmax(a),v))
}
gelu <- function(x,approximate=FALSE) {
  # TensorFlow's native exact-GELU path casts 1/sqrt(2) through float32;
  # that loses float64 derivative accuracy. Write the same formula directly.
  if(!approximate)return(x*scalar(.5,x)*(1+tf$math$erf(x/tf$sqrt(scalar(2,x)))))
  # GPT-2's declared tanh approximation. Construct constants directly in the
  # operand dtype: tf.cast(Python-float,float64) first rounds through float32.
  x*scalar(.5,x)*(1+tf$tanh(scalar(sqrt(2/pi),x)*(x+scalar(.044715,x)*x^3)))
}

# %% Load public pretrained weights without hiding a different training program

# %% Scalar-output covariance: retain every first-order weight direction
# For the binary contrast z=f_positive-f_negative, Var(z) is sum(J_l^2 v_l).
# A reverse sensitivity contracts this sum without an input-by-input matrix.
# Below, each little operation has its own VJP. Reversing this calculation
# differentiates the variance as well as the mean; no whole-model gradient is
# substituted for the candidate's explicit message traversal.
scalar_moment_forward<-function(g,x,ms,vs,record=TRUE,retain_jacobian=FALSE) {
  n<-length(ms);values<-c(ms,vs,list(x));tapes<-list()
  add<-function(parents,fn) {
    ids<-unique(parents);ix<-match(parents,ids);inputs<-values[ids]
    if(record) {
      with(tf$GradientTape(watch_accessed_variables=FALSE) %as% tape, {
        tape$watch(inputs);out<-fn(inputs[ix])
      })
    } else out<-fn(inputs[ix])
    new<-length(values)+seq_along(out)
    values<<-c(values,out)
    if(record)tapes[[length(tapes)+1L]]<<-list(tape=tape,inputs=inputs,outputs=out,parents=ids,children=new)
    new
  }
  # Forward means at the current weight means.
  boundary<-c(2L*n+1L)
  for(op in g$nodes) {
    np<-length(op$parents);nw<-length(op$weights)
    boundary<-c(boundary,add(c(boundary[op$parents],op$weights),function(a)
      list(op$point(a[seq_len(np)],if(nw)a[np+seq_len(nw)] else list()))))
  }
  mean_id<-add(tail(boundary,1),function(a)list(tf$gather(a[[1]],1L,axis=1L)-tf$gather(a[[1]],0L,axis=1L)))
  signal<-rep(NA_integer_,length(boundary))
  signal[[length(boundary)]]<-add(tail(boundary,1),function(a)
    list(tf$ones_like(a[[1]])*tf$constant(c(-1,1),dtype=a[[1]]$dtype)))
  contributions<-integer();jacobian_ids<-rep(NA_integer_,n)
  # Backward sensitivities, adding all contributions at a shared parent.
  for(j in rev(seq_along(g$nodes))) {
    op<-g$nodes[[j]];sid<-signal[[j+1L]]
    if(is.na(sid))next
    if(op$kind=="lora") {
      stopifnot(length(op$parents)==1L,length(op$weights)==2L)
      A<-op$weights[[1]];B<-op$weights[[2]];scale<-op$lora_scale
      answer<-add(c(boundary[op$parents],A,B,sid,n+A,n+B),function(a) {
        H<-a[[1]];W_A<-a[[2]];W_B<-a[[3]];S<-a[[4]]
        SB<-tf$matmul(S,W_B,transpose_b=TRUE)
        J_A<-scale*tf$einsum("bti,btj->bij",H,SB)
        J_B<-scale*tf$einsum("bti,btj->bij",tf$matmul(H,W_A),S)
        variance<-tf$reduce_sum(J_A^2*a[[5]],axis=c(1L,2L))+
                  tf$reduce_sum(J_B^2*a[[6]],axis=c(1L,2L))
        parent<-tf$matmul(S,op$frozen_weight,transpose_b=TRUE)+
                scale*tf$matmul(SB,W_A,transpose_b=TRUE)
        if(retain_jacobian)list(parent,variance,J_A,J_B) else list(parent,variance)
      })
      parent_signals<-answer[[1]];contributions<-c(contributions,answer[[2]])
      if(retain_jacobian) {jacobian_ids[[A]]<-answer[[3]];jacobian_ids[[B]]<-answer[[4]]}
    } else {
      stopifnot(length(op$weights)==0L)
      # Transformers have no cross-example operations here. The VJP of the
      # batched map therefore supplies one sensitivity per input example.
      ids<-unique(op$parents);ix<-match(op$parents,ids);k<-length(ids)
      parent_signals<-add(c(boundary[ids],sid),function(a) {
        parents<-a[seq_len(k)]
        with(tf$GradientTape(watch_accessed_variables=FALSE) %as% pull, {
          pull$watch(parents);out<-op$point(parents[ix],list())
        })
        as_r(pull$gradient(out,parents,output_gradients=a[[k+1L]],
          unconnected_gradients=tf$UnconnectedGradients$ZERO))
      })
      # Repeated parents were differentiated together; do not count twice.
      op$parents<-ids
    }
    for(k in seq_along(op$parents)) {
      p<-op$parents[[k]];s<-parent_signals[[k]]
      signal[[p]]<-if(is.na(signal[[p]]))s else
        add(c(signal[[p]],s),function(a)list(a[[1]]+a[[2]]))
    }
  }
  stopifnot(length(contributions)>0L)
  variance_id<-add(contributions,function(a)list(Reduce(`+`,a)))
  list(mean=values[[mean_id]],variance=values[[variance_id]],mean_id=mean_id,
       variance_id=variance_id,values=values,tapes=tapes,n=n,
       jacobians=if(retain_jacobian)values[jacobian_ids] else NULL)
}
scalar_moment_reverse<-function(f,gm,gv) {
  adj<-vector("list",length(f$values));adj[[f$mean_id]]<-gm;adj[[f$variance_id]]<-gv
  for(a in rev(f$tapes)) {
    child<-lapply(a$children,function(i)if(is.null(adj[[i]]))zero(f$values[[i]]) else adj[[i]])
    d<-as_r(a$tape$gradient(a$outputs,a$inputs,output_gradients=child,
      unconnected_gradients=tf$UnconnectedGradients$ZERO))
    for(k in seq_along(a$parents)) {
      i<-a$parents[[k]];adj[[i]]<-if(is.null(adj[[i]]))d[[k]] else adj[[i]]+d[[k]]
    }
  }
  get<-function(i)if(is.null(adj[[i]]))zero(f$values[[i]]) else adj[[i]]
  list(gm=lapply(seq_len(f$n),get),gv=lapply(f$n+seq_len(f$n),get))
}

# %% Binary Gaussian head: integrate probabilities, not logits
# Gauss-Hermite nodes integrate the declared scalar Gaussian contrast. They
# are quadrature points, not sampled whole networks or independent token logits.
binary_gaussian_head<-function(m,v,y,expected=FALSE,order=20L) {
  rule<-as_r(np$polynomial$hermite$hermgauss(as.integer(order)))
  nodes<-tf$constant(as.numeric(rule[[1]])*sqrt(2),dtype=m$dtype)
  weights<-tf$constant(as.numeric(rule[[2]])/sqrt(pi),dtype=m$dtype)
  z<-tf$expand_dims(m,1L)+tf$expand_dims(tf$sqrt(v),1L)*nodes
  signed<-tf$expand_dims(2*tf$cast(y,m$dtype)-1,1L)*z
  logp<--tf$math$softplus(-signed)
  loss<-if(expected)-tf$reduce_mean(tf$reduce_sum(logp*weights,axis=1L)) else
    -tf$reduce_mean(tf$reduce_logsumexp(logp+tf$math$log(weights),axis=1L))
  positive<-tf$reduce_sum(tf$math$sigmoid(z)*weights,axis=1L)
  list(loss=loss,probabilities=tf$stack(list(1-positive,positive),axis=1L))
}

# %% Frozen-Jacobian MFVI: correlated minibatch gradient moments, not E[g]^2
gaussian_residual_moments<-function(m,C,y,order=20L) {
  # r_i=sigmoid(z_i)-y_i. The SAME uncertain weights generate every z_i.
  # Hence E[g_j^2]=J_j' E[rr'] J_j/B^2, including cross-example terms.
  rule<-as_r(np$polynomial$hermite$hermgauss(as.integer(order)))
  t<-tf$constant(as.numeric(rule[[1]])*sqrt(2),dtype=m$dtype)
  w<-tf$constant(as.numeric(rule[[2]])/sqrt(pi),dtype=m$dtype)
  sd<-tf$sqrt(tf$maximum(tf$linalg$diag_part(C),zero(m)))
  outer<-tf$einsum("i,j->ij",sd,sd)
  correlation<-tf$where(outer>0,C/tf$maximum(outer,scalar(1e-30,outer)),zero(outer))
  tf$debugging$assert_less_equal(tf$reduce_max(tf$abs(correlation)),scalar(1+1e-5,m))
  correlation<-tf$clip_by_value(correlation,scalar(-1,m),scalar(1,m))
  residual<-tf$math$sigmoid(tf$expand_dims(m,1L)+tf$expand_dims(sd,1L)*t)-
              tf$expand_dims(tf$cast(y,m$dtype),1L)
  first<-tf$reduce_sum(residual*w,axis=1L)
  # Shape [i,j,t,u]; integrate the bivariate Gaussian for each example pair.
  rho<-tf$expand_dims(tf$expand_dims(correlation,2L),3L)
  tj<-tf$reshape(t,c(1L,1L,order,1L));uj<-tf$reshape(t,c(1L,1L,1L,order))
  zj<-tf$reshape(m,c(1L,-1L,1L,1L))+tf$reshape(sd,c(1L,-1L,1L,1L))*
       (rho*tj+tf$sqrt(tf$maximum(1-rho^2,zero(rho)))*uj)
  rj<-tf$math$sigmoid(zj)-tf$reshape(tf$cast(y,m$dtype),c(1L,-1L,1L,1L))
  second<-tf$reduce_sum(tf$expand_dims(tf$expand_dims(residual,1L),3L)*rj*
    tf$reshape(w,c(1L,1L,order,1L))*tf$reshape(w,c(1L,1L,1L,order)),axis=c(2L,3L))
  second<-(second+tf$transpose(second))/2
  second<-tf$linalg$set_diag(second,tf$reduce_sum(residual^2*w,axis=1L))
  list(first=first,second=second)
}
frozen_gradient_moments<-function(m,J,vs,y,order=20L) {
  # J is recomputed at EACH current mean, then held fixed for this update.
  # Only the small minibatch covariance and contractions use float64.
  B<-tf$gather(tf$shape(m),0L);Bd<-tf$cast(B,tf$float64)
  flat<-lapply(J,function(j)tf$cast(tf$reshape(j,tf$stack(list(B,-1L))),tf$float64))
  vv<-lapply(vs,function(v)tf$cast(tf$reshape(v,tuple(-1L)),tf$float64))
  C<-Reduce(`+`,Map(function(j,v)tf$matmul(j*v,j,transpose_b=TRUE),flat,vv))
  r<-gaussian_residual_moments(tf$cast(m,tf$float64),C,y,order)
  gm<-Map(function(j,v)tf$reshape(tf$linalg$matvec(j,r$first,transpose_a=TRUE)/Bd,tf$shape(v)),flat,vs)
  g2<-Map(function(j,v)tf$reshape(tf$reduce_sum(j*tf$matmul(r$second,j),axis=0L)/(Bd^2),tf$shape(v)),flat,vs)
  maximum<-tf$reduce_max(tf$stack(lapply(g2,function(a)tf$reduce_max(tf$abs(a)))))
  minimum<-tf$reduce_min(tf$stack(lapply(g2,tf$reduce_min)))
  tf$debugging$assert_greater_equal(minimum,-tf$maximum(scalar(1e-24,maximum),scalar(1e-10,maximum)*maximum),
    message="Gaussian quadrature produced a materially negative gradient second moment.")
  list(gm=Map(function(a,v)tf$cast(a,v$dtype),gm,vs),
       g2=Map(function(a,v)tf$cast(tf$maximum(a,zero(a)),v$dtype),g2,vs),C=C)
}

# %% Frozen local Jacobians: propagate several output sensitivities on one DAG
frozen_graph_reverse<-function(g,states,ms,seeds) {
  # Each seed is an output adjoint. The first gives E[g]; the others give
  # J' H_loss J delta_w. No derivative of J is included in this closure.
  ns<-length(seeds);adj<-lapply(seeds,function(a) {
    v<-vector("list",length(states));v[[length(v)]]<-a;v
  })
  gradients<-lapply(seeds,function(a)lapply(ms,zero))
  for(j in rev(seq_along(g$nodes))) {
    op<-g$nodes[[j]];parents<-unique(op$parents);ix<-match(op$parents,parents)
    parameters<-unique(op$weights);wi<-match(op$weights,parameters)
    inputs<-c(lapply(states[parents],`[[`,"m"),ms[parameters]);np<-length(parents);nw<-length(parameters)
    with(tf$GradientTape(persistent=TRUE,watch_accessed_variables=FALSE) %as% tape, {
      tape$watch(inputs)
      output<-op$point(inputs[ix],if(nw)inputs[np+wi] else list())
    })
    for(s in seq_len(ns)) {
      if(is.null(adj[[s]][[j+1L]]))next
      d<-dense_gradients(tape$gradient(output,inputs,output_gradients=adj[[s]][[j+1L]],
                            unconnected_gradients=tf$UnconnectedGradients$ZERO))
      for(k in seq_along(parents)) {
        p<-parents[[k]]
        adj[[s]][[p]]<-if(is.null(adj[[s]][[p]]))d[[k]] else adj[[s]][[p]]+d[[k]]
      }
      for(k in seq_along(parameters)) {
        p<-parameters[[k]];gradients[[s]][[p]]<-gradients[[s]][[p]]+d[[np+k]]
      }
    }
  }
  gradients
}
frozen_shared_statistics<-function(g,x,ms,vs,y) {
  f<-moment_forward(g,x,ms,vs,record=FALSE)
  h<-head_backward(f$output,y,"mfvi",1,normals=g$head_normals)
  p<-tf$nn$softmax(f$output$m);B<-tf$cast(tf$gather(tf$shape(p),0L),p$dtype)
  # Hessian of categorical cross-entropy: diag(p)-p p'.
  variation<-lapply(f$output$U,function(u) {
    u<-u/sqrt(g$rank)
    p*(u-tf$reduce_sum(p*u,axis=1L,keepdims=TRUE))/B
  })
  gradients<-frozen_graph_reverse(g,f$states,ms,c(list(h$adj[[1]]),variation))
  first<-gradients[[1]]
  second<-lapply(seq_along(ms),function(i)first[[i]]^2+
    Reduce(`+`,lapply(gradients[-1],function(a)a[[i]]^2)))
  list(gm=first,g2=second,loss=h$loss,forward=f)
}

build_gpt2_lora <- function(rank=4L,seed=41L,public=NULL,dtype=tf$float32) {
  if(is.null(public)) public<-load_public_weights("openai-community/gpt2")
  tf$random$set_seed(as.integer(seed));g<-new_graph(rank,seed);g$training<-FALSE
  g$prior_center<-"zero"
  W<-function(name)tf$cast(public$get(name),dtype)
  emb<-W("wte.weight");pos<-W("wpe.weight")
  x<-node(g,"embedding",1L,function(xs,ws) {
    ids<-tf$cast(tf$gather(xs[[1]],0L,axis=2L),tf$int32)
    n<-tf$gather(tf$shape(ids),1L)
    tf$gather(emb,ids)+tf$gather(pos,tf$range(n))
  })
  frozen_ln<-function(x,p) {
    a<-W(paste0(p,".weight"));b<-W(paste0(p,".bias"))
    node(g,p,x,function(xs,ws)layer_norm(xs[[1]],a,b,1e-5))
  }
  frozen_dense<-function(x,a,b,p) {
    a<-tf$identity(a);b<-tf$identity(b)
    node(g,p,x,function(xs,ws)tf$matmul(xs[[1]],a)+b)
  }
  for(i in 0:11) {
    p<-paste0("h.",i);r<-x;x<-frozen_ln(x,paste0(p,".ln_1"))
    a<-W(paste0(p,".attn.c_attn.weight"));b<-W(paste0(p,".attn.c_attn.bias"))
    aa<-as_r(tf$split(a,3L,axis=1L));bb<-as_r(tf$split(b,3L,axis=0L))
    qkv<-integer(3)
    for(j in 1:3) {
      a0<-aa[[j]];b0<-bb[[j]];pn<-paste0(p,c(".query",".key",".value")[[j]])
      if(j==2L) qkv[[j]]<-frozen_dense(x,a0,b0,pn) else {
        ia<-weight(g,paste0(pn,"_A"),normal(c(768L,4L),.02,dtype),1e-6,1/2500)
        ib<-weight(g,paste0(pn,"_B"),tf$zeros(c(4L,768L),dtype=dtype),1e-6,1/2500)
        qkv[[j]]<-node(g,pn,x,local({a0<-a0;b0<-b0;function(xs,ws) {
          tf$matmul(xs[[1]],a0)+b0+8*tf$matmul(tf$matmul(xs[[1]],ws[[1]]),ws[[2]])
        }}),c(ia,ib),kind="lora")
        g$nodes[[qkv[[j]]-1L]]$frozen_weight<-a0
        g$nodes[[qkv[[j]]-1L]]$lora_scale<-8
      }
    }
    x<-node(g,paste0(p,".attention"),c(qkv,1L),function(xs,ws)attention(xs[[1]],xs[[2]],xs[[3]],xs[[4]],TRUE))
    x<-frozen_dense(x,W(paste0(p,".attn.c_proj.weight")),W(paste0(p,".attn.c_proj.bias")),paste0(p,".attn.out"))
    x<-add_node(g,r,x,paste0(p,".attention_residual"));r<-x
    x<-frozen_ln(x,paste0(p,".ln_2"))
    x<-frozen_dense(x,W(paste0(p,".mlp.c_fc.weight")),W(paste0(p,".mlp.c_fc.bias")),paste0(p,".mlp.in"))
    x<-node(g,paste0(p,".gelu"),x,function(xs,ws)gelu(xs[[1]],TRUE))
    x<-frozen_dense(x,W(paste0(p,".mlp.c_proj.weight")),W(paste0(p,".mlp.c_proj.bias")),paste0(p,".mlp.out"))
    x<-add_node(g,r,x,paste0(p,".mlp_residual"))
  }
  x<-frozen_ln(x,"ln_f")
  # These token IDs are obtained and checked from the public tokenizer below.
  tokenizer<-import("transformers",convert=FALSE)$AutoTokenizer$from_pretrained("openai-community/gpt2",
    revision="607a30d783dfa663caf39e06633721c8d4cfcd7e",token=FALSE)
  tokenizer$pad_token<-tokenizer$eos_token;tokenizer$padding_side<-"right"
  tokens<-lapply(c(" negative"," positive"),function(s)as.integer(as_r(tokenizer$encode(s,add_special_tokens=FALSE))))
  stopifnot(all(lengths(tokens)==1L));g$verbalizer<-unlist(tokens)
  V<-tf$gather(emb,as.integer(g$verbalizer))
  node(g,"binary_verbalizer",c(x,1L),function(xs,ws) {
    mask<-tf$gather(xs[[2]],1L,axis=2L)
    index<-tf$cast(tf$reduce_sum(mask,axis=1L)-1,tf$int32)
    h<-tf$gather(xs[[1]],index,axis=1L,batch_dims=1L)
    tf$matmul(h,V,transpose_b=TRUE)
  })
  g$architecture<-"gpt2_small_qv_lora4";g$tokenizer<-tokenizer;g$public_path<-public$path;g
}

# %% RoBERTa-base: full 12-block encoder and 150-class CLINC head

GPT-2 with LoRA: SST-2 sentiment classification

GPT-2-small uses rank-4 query/value adapters and a frozen verbalizer head; predictions average class probabilities. The reporting cohort contains 872 SST-2 examples. The table retains the strong saved EP and MFVI predictors. Epochs are explicit: each Bayesian row’s time ratio uses the ordinary row from its own training protocol, not a slower or less accurate reference chosen from another run. This is a comparison of saved fitted predictors, not an optimizer-only ablation. All displayed training and prediction times are A100 measurements; prediction processes the full reporting cohort.

The one-epoch sampled MFVI uses 16 networks for prediction. Moment EP uses the first-order predictor and the tied power-EP objective optimized by Adam on Gaussian mean and log variance. The three-epoch moment MFVI uses the single-Gaussian conditional-carrier construction just described: learning rate 3×10−43\times10^{-4}, prior/variance SGD rate 0.002, batch 32, seed 41, and the source cyclic KL schedule. Its native predictor uses one correlated direction. These are distinct update approximations to the earlier literal message-passing identities. The source configurations and additional saved prediction ablations remain packaged with the probability arrays.

The following tables recompute uncertainty statistics from the original per-example probability records. The collapsed training cells preserve the original Python/PyTorch implementation for these selected fits.

GPT-2-small + rank-4 LoRA / SST-2

The decoder box contains twelve pre-normalized transformer blocks. Query/value adapters have rank four; the frozen tied readout selects the negative/positive token logits.

Original transformer training implementation

These complete source cells preserve the code that trained the displayed transformer beliefs. The first SST-2 comparison uses the archived Vadam/MFVI recurrence and tied-power-EP energy with Adam. The later SST-2 and CLINC examples use the BLoB-inspired split AdamW/SGD update with conditional activation moments. The public BLoB dependency is fixed to commit 7d960082; the source manifest records the source versions and portable file-path changes. Training runs only when its switch is enabled.

Results. Moment EP reaches 92.32% accuracy / 0.22336 NLL, versus its ordinary comparator’s 91.97% / 0.22739. The stronger moment-MFVI predictor reaches 91.86% / 0.21489, with 2.02% ECE and about 2.19 times its corresponding ordinary prediction cost. The ordinary three-epoch endpoint is more overconfident; its earlier epoch-1 NLL was 0.21775, so the large endpoint improvement is not a claim to beat every ordinary stopping rule.

The same four panels used for the image models show reliability, selective prediction and error-detection ROC. The positive ROC event is an incorrect decision, scored by 1−max⁡cp‾c1-\max_c\bar p_c. The table includes its AUROC; it is not an OOD test. Improved NLL or ECE need not improve every error-ranking metric. The stronger four-direction EP prediction (92.28% / 0.21144, averaged over three saved direction seeds) remains in the supplied ablation table, without pooling those seeds into an extra ensemble curve.

Independent replay of the same Gaussian adapters

The selected Gaussian A+B MFVI and EP beliefs above are also evaluated by the original PyTorch implementation and a separate native JAX implementation. They use identical pretrained weights, 872 SST-2 inputs and a 20-node Gaussian integral. For the logit contrast z(w)z(w), both use mz=z(m)m_z=z(m) and vz=∑j(∂jz(m))2vjv_z=\sum_j(\partial_j z(m))^2v_j, including the derivative of the Jacobian in the backward pass. All adapter mean and variance derivatives are compared at four fixed examples, without another optimizer step or training run. The check uses the fully differentiated map; a frozen-Jacobian training variant is a separate approximation.

This is an explicitly PyTorch/JAX reference comparison, displayed here beside the original Python transformer sources. It is not an R training result. Matching the same approximation establishes implementation agreement; the earlier Monte Carlo experiment separately measures approximation error.

7. Conditional moments and RoBERTa / CLINC150

RoBERTa-base with LoRA: CLINC150 intent classification

RoBERTa-base has rank-8 query/value adapters, scale 1, and a point classifier. Only adapter AA is Gaussian; embeddings, backbone and adapter BB are not given a Bayesian distribution. The model trains on 13,500 examples and selects its checkpoint using 1,500 training-derived stopping examples; the displayed fits select epoch 6. Evaluation uses 4,500 official in-domain test examples. Batch size is 32 and seed is 41. Mean learning rate is 0.001 with 6% warmup and linear decay; prior/variance SGD starts at 0.002. The prior, cyclic KL and conditional carriers are the same construction described above.

Complete training times below were recorded on L4. Optimized inference times were measured on A100, for both models; they are not mixed within a time ratio. The moment predictor uses two tangent directions and averages softmax probabilities. It is one Gaussian belief, not an ensemble of trained networks. The comparison here concerns LoRA, not full-weight Bayesian fine tuning.

R/TensorFlow architecture. The released constructor shares the attention, normalization, GELU and graph operations already used in this tutorial. It implements xW0+b0+(xA)BxW_0+b_0+(xA)B, with Gaussian AA, point BB and a point classifier. The point variables are stored separately from the Gaussian factors. Its Keras view reuses these same operations and variables. The reported fit uses the separately included Python training implementation.

Download fully expanded model (PDF) · Full native layer summary.

The independent execution check uses nonzero adapters, padded batches and five/eight-token inputs: 28 activation/logit comparisons pass; the maximum logit discrepancy is 1.87×10−71.87\times10^{-7} in float32. The native Keras view itself matches the R graph exactly. The saved native-view checks are in the architecture receipt.

The complete R model construction is printed below. The original training implementation is included separately and explicitly labeled.

build_roberta <- function(rank=4L,seed=41L,public=NULL,dtype=tf$float32) {
  if(is.null(public)) public<-load_public_weights("FacebookAI/roberta-base")
  tf$random$set_seed(as.integer(seed));g<-new_graph(rank,seed);g$training<-FALSE
  W<-function(name)tf$cast(public$get(name),dtype)
  parameter<-function(p,transpose=FALSE) {
    a<-W(p);if(transpose) a<-tf$transpose(a)
    i<-weight(g,gsub("\\.","_",p),a,variance=1e-8,prior_variance=1e-6)
    g$weights[[i]]$source_name<-p;g$weights[[i]]$source_transpose<-transpose;i
  }
  ids<-sapply(c("roberta.embeddings.word_embeddings.weight","roberta.embeddings.position_embeddings.weight",
               "roberta.embeddings.token_type_embeddings.weight"),parameter)
  x<-node(g,"embedding",1L,function(xs,ws) {
    t<-tf$cast(tf$gather(xs[[1]],0L,axis=2L),tf$int32)
    mask<-tf$cast(tf$not_equal(t,1L),tf$int32)
    pos<-tf$cumsum(mask,axis=1L)*mask+1L
    tf$gather(ws[[1]],t)+tf$gather(ws[[2]],pos)+tf$gather(ws[[3]],0L)
  },ids)
  norm_node<-function(x,p) {
    ids<-c(parameter(paste0(p,".weight")),parameter(paste0(p,".bias")))
    node(g,p,x,function(xs,ws)layer_norm(xs[[1]],ws[[1]],ws[[2]],1e-5),ids)
  }
  linear<-function(x,p) {
    ids<-c(parameter(paste0(p,".weight"),TRUE),parameter(paste0(p,".bias")))
    node(g,p,x,function(xs,ws)tf$matmul(xs[[1]],ws[[1]])+ws[[2]],ids)
  }
  x<-norm_node(x,"roberta.embeddings.LayerNorm")
  for(i in 0:11) {
    p<-paste0("roberta.encoder.layer.",i);skip<-x
    q<-linear(x,paste0(p,".attention.self.query"))
    k<-linear(x,paste0(p,".attention.self.key"))
    v<-linear(x,paste0(p,".attention.self.value"))
    x<-node(g,paste0(p,".attention"),c(q,k,v,1L),function(xs,ws)attention(xs[[1]],xs[[2]],xs[[3]],xs[[4]],FALSE))
    x<-linear(x,paste0(p,".attention.output.dense"))
    x<-norm_node(add_node(g,skip,x,paste0(p,".residual1")),paste0(p,".attention.output.LayerNorm"));skip<-x
    x<-linear(x,paste0(p,".intermediate.dense"))
    x<-node(g,paste0(p,".gelu"),x,function(xs,ws)gelu(xs[[1]]))
    x<-linear(x,paste0(p,".output.dense"))
    x<-norm_node(add_node(g,skip,x,paste0(p,".residual2")),paste0(p,".output.LayerNorm"))
  }
  x<-node(g,"CLS",x,function(xs,ws)tf$gather(xs[[1]],0L,axis=1L))
  linear_head<-function(x,input,output,name,key) {
    iw<-weight(g,paste0(name,"_weight"),normal(c(input,output),.02,dtype),1e-8,1e-6)
    ib<-weight(g,paste0(name,"_bias"),tf$zeros(c(output),dtype=dtype),1e-8,1e-6)
    g$weights[[iw]]$source_name<-paste0(key,".weight");g$weights[[iw]]$source_transpose<-TRUE
    g$weights[[ib]]$source_name<-paste0(key,".bias");g$weights[[ib]]$source_transpose<-FALSE
    node(g,name,x,function(xs,ws)tf$matmul(xs[[1]],ws[[1]])+ws[[2]],c(iw,ib))
  }
  x<-linear_head(x,768L,768L,"classifier_dense","classifier.dense")
  x<-node(g,"classifier_tanh",x,function(xs,ws)tf$tanh(xs[[1]]))
  # The historical RoBERTa contract uses the shared first-order factors through
  # the full classifier, not the CIFAR conditional-Gaussian readout closure.
  linear_head(x,768L,150L,"classifier_out","classifier.out_proj")
  g$architecture<-"roberta_base_full";g$public_path<-public$path
  g$tokenizer<-import("transformers",convert=FALSE)$AutoTokenizer$from_pretrained("FacebookAI/roberta-base",
    revision="e2da8e2f811d1448a5b465c236feacd80ffbac7b",token=FALSE)
  g
}
# RoBERTa-LoRA: fixed backbone, Gaussian A, point B and point classifier.
# For a row activation x, a query/value map is x W0 + b0 + (x A) B.
# A is 768-by-r; B is r-by-768. Here alpha/r = 8/8 = 1.
# The same graph supports point_forward() and the shared-factor moment pass.
build_roberta_lora <- function(rank=4L,seed=41L,public=NULL,dtype=tf$float32) {
  if(is.null(public))public<-load_public_weights("FacebookAI/roberta-base")
  tf$random$set_seed(as.integer(seed))
  g<-new_graph(rank,seed);g$training<-FALSE;g$prior_center<-"zero"
  g$point_weights<-list()
  fixed<-function(name,transpose=FALSE) {
    a<-tf$cast(public$get(name),dtype)
    if(transpose)a<-tf$transpose(a)
    tf$Variable(a,trainable=FALSE,name=gsub("\\.","_",name))
  }
  point_parameter<-function(name,a) {
    w<-tf$Variable(a,name=gsub("\\.","_",name))
    g$point_weights[[name]]<-w;w
  }
  emb<-fixed("roberta.embeddings.word_embeddings.weight")
  pos<-fixed("roberta.embeddings.position_embeddings.weight")
  typ<-fixed("roberta.embeddings.token_type_embeddings.weight")
  x<-node(g,"embedding",1L,function(xs,ws) {
    ids<-tf$cast(tf$gather(xs[[1]],0L,axis=2L),tf$int32)
    mask<-tf$cast(tf$not_equal(ids,1L),tf$int32)
    positions<-tf$cumsum(mask,axis=1L)*mask+1L
    tf$gather(emb,ids)+tf$gather(pos,positions)+tf$gather(typ,0L)
  })
  norm<-function(x,name) {
    force(x)
    a<-fixed(paste0(name,".weight"));b<-fixed(paste0(name,".bias"))
    node(g,name,x,function(xs,ws)layer_norm(xs[[1]],a,b,1e-5))
  }
  linear<-function(x,name,lora=FALSE) {
    force(x)
    a<-fixed(paste0(name,".weight"),TRUE);b<-fixed(paste0(name,".bias"))
    if(!lora)return(node(g,name,x,function(xs,ws)tf$matmul(xs[[1]],a)+b))
    # PEFT's A initializer; B starts at zero. rho^2 is the standard deviation.
    A<-tf$random$uniform(c(768L,8L),minval=-1/sqrt(768),maxval=1/sqrt(768),dtype=dtype)
    i<-weight(g,paste0(name,"_A"),A,variance=1e-6,prior_variance=.2^2)
    rho<-tf$random$uniform(c(768L,8L),minval=.05/sqrt(2),maxval=.05,dtype=dtype)
    g$weights[[i]]$lv$assign(4*tf$math$log(rho))
    g$weights[[i]]$source_name<-paste0(name,".lora_A")
    B<-point_parameter(paste0(name,".lora_B"),tf$zeros(c(8L,768L),dtype=dtype))
    node(g,name,x,function(xs,ws)
      tf$matmul(xs[[1]],a)+b+tf$matmul(tf$matmul(xs[[1]],ws[[1]]),B),i)
  }
  x<-norm(x,"roberta.embeddings.LayerNorm")
  for(i in 0:11) {
    p<-paste0("roberta.encoder.layer.",i);skip<-x
    q<-linear(x,paste0(p,".attention.self.query"),TRUE)
    k<-linear(x,paste0(p,".attention.self.key"))
    v<-linear(x,paste0(p,".attention.self.value"),TRUE)
    x<-node(g,paste0(p,".attention"),c(q,k,v,1L),function(xs,ws)
      attention(xs[[1]],xs[[2]],xs[[3]],xs[[4]],FALSE))
    x<-linear(x,paste0(p,".attention.output.dense"))
    x<-norm(add_node(g,skip,x,paste0(p,".residual1")),paste0(p,".attention.output.LayerNorm"));skip<-x
    x<-linear(x,paste0(p,".intermediate.dense"))
    x<-node(g,paste0(p,".gelu"),x,function(xs,ws)gelu(xs[[1]]))
    x<-linear(x,paste0(p,".output.dense"))
    x<-norm(add_node(g,skip,x,paste0(p,".residual2")),paste0(p,".output.LayerNorm"))
  }
  x<-node(g,"CLS",x,function(xs,ws)tf$gather(xs[[1]],0L,axis=1L))
  head<-function(x,input,output,name) {
    force(x)
    a<-point_parameter(paste0(name,".weight"),normal(c(input,output),.02,dtype))
    b<-point_parameter(paste0(name,".bias"),tf$zeros(c(output),dtype=dtype))
    node(g,name,x,function(xs,ws)tf$matmul(xs[[1]],a)+b)
  }
  x<-head(x,768L,768L,"classifier.dense")
  x<-node(g,"classifier.tanh",x,function(xs,ws)tf$tanh(xs[[1]]))
  head(x,768L,150L,"classifier.out_proj")
  g$architecture<-"roberta_lora8";g$public_path<-public$path;g
}

Results. Moment MFVI reaches 96.60% accuracy / 0.14172 NLL, versus 96.22% / 0.14990 for ordinary AdamW, and reduces ECE from 0.99% to 0.72%. Native prediction costs about 2.61 times the ordinary pass. The four-panel diagnostic uses the same definitions and layout as CIFAR-10. Error-detection AUROC is slightly lower (0.9421 versus 0.9472), so the measured benefit is better predictive accuracy and probability calibration, not a universal improvement in every uncertainty ranking. These saved fits do not establish across-training-seed significance.

8. Reproduction and code reading

The experiments answer three distinct questions.

  1. Inference identities: the Gaussian fixture agrees with independent conditioning; literal EP/MFVI derivatives agree with pseudo-gradient transport for the same stated forward map and objective. MFVI and EP need not have the same variance target.
  2. Approximation fidelity: retaining covariance can improve forward moments. Backward accuracy must also be measured, including isolated variance signals. More integration directions trade computation for approximation quality; an MC comparison is not another posterior model or a proof of posterior exactness.
  3. Predictive usefulness: held-out probabilities establish accuracy, calibration, ranking and cost for the named fitted predictors. These metrics are complementary; a gain in one does not imply gains on every OOD dataset.

Code reading map

Reader’s task Released source What to follow
Gaussian identity and exact conditioning R/gaussian.R Coordinate conversion and an independent reference
One forward/backward sweep R/layers.R Cached maps, local VJP and shared-parent accumulation
EP versus MFVI R/messages.R, R/inference.R Different objectives and finite updates; common message coordinates
Correlated activations and sensitivities R/covariance.R Shared directions and the nonlinear residual calculation
Build the networks R/models.R Complete MLP, LeNet, ResNet, DenseNet and transformer constructors
Follow training and prediction R/inference.R, R/experiments.R Optimizer recurrences, fixed data/schedules, probability averaging
Uncertainty statistics and plots R/uncertainty.R, R/plots.R Common metrics and diagnostic drawing functions
Check identities and recover results R/checks.R, R/results.R Independent comparisons and raw-record readers
Original transformer fits python/gpt2, python/blob_mirror The actual Python/PyTorch training and prediction sources

The handwritten message calculations serve as independent references. Diagonal versus shared-direction covariance changes the approximation used on the graph. Specialized convolution and scalar-readout routines make their computation explicit; they do not change EP’s normalizer into MFVI’s expected log likelihood.

Reproduction

Restart Kernel and Run All runs the small mathematical checks and fixed-reference figures, then displays the labeled recorded benchmark outputs. The compact supplement includes metric tables, histories and plot coordinates in results/, but no model checkpoints or bulk prediction arrays. Enable the public-data training switches to regenerate fits and per-example predictions using the included implementation. A runtime or training failure is not replaced by a historical score.

The source map gives each complete definition’s file, line range and visibility. Cell metadata also records source hashes. The section guide lists code counts, purposes and dependencies. All images follow their generating call. HTML collapses support code; the native-LaTeX PDF prints the complete teaching definitions at 9.2 points, with 10-point text and mathematics. Fully expanded architecture PDFs are separate vector diagrams for zooming.

This source consolidation was checked with clean Consumer Colab execution, independent Gaussian/EP/MFVI numerical comparisons, image-model updates, original-transformer dependency and update checks, and raw-record replay. No new benchmark scores or GPU timing claims are created by packaging these files.
